editorial.title: The New Supply Chain Risk Is Dependency
editorial.dek: The real resilience question is no longer how much capacity exists, but how many practical ways cargo can move when preferred routes stop behaving normally.
body: The question, “How much capacity is available?” is becoming increasingly irrelevant.

This week alone, logistics networks were dealing with severe port congestion in East Asia, new operational pressure around the Strait of Hormuz, and further restrictions at the Panama Canal. None of these situations mean the world has suddenly run out of ships, terminals, trucks or infrastructure. The problem is that too much cargo still depends on a relatively small number of routes, gateways and operating assumptions.

At Shanghai and Ningbo, successive typhoons have created vessel queues stretching several days. Global containership capacity waiting to berth reached about 4.31 million TEU, with Shanghai waiting times reported as high as 12 days at some terminals. A leading carrier has already omitted Shanghai calls on certain voyages to protect onward schedules.

With this year’s lower-than-expected rainfall, the Panama Canal Authority announced reduced daily transit capacity beginning in September. It has also been adjusting draft restrictions and its booking system as water conditions change. Access to the Canal is becoming more conditional, particularly for vessels without secured reservations.
Then there is the Strait of Hormuz. This week, Iran threatened penalties, detention and possible cargo confiscation against dozens of tankers it says violated its transit requirements.
One is weather. One is water availability. One is geopolitics.
Operationally, however, they expose the same weakness.
Supply chains that run efficiently through preferred routes are often much less efficient when those routes stop behaving normally.
That changes how resilience should be measured.

A company may have three carriers, but if all three depend on the same transshipment hub, the diversification is mostly cosmetic. A shipper may have several suppliers, but if all of them export through the same congested gateway, the risk remains concentrated. If alternatives only become visible after the primary routing fails, they are contingency plans rather than real options.
How much capacity do you have?
How many practical ways do you have to move your cargo?
That means looking beyond freight rates and transit times when planning important shipments.
Efficiency matters. None of this means abandoning it.
But the cheapest or fastest routing on a normal day is not necessarily the lowest-cost routing across the life of a shipment.
A supply chain with one perfect route is efficient. A supply chain with three workable routes is resilient.

items.title: Mundra empty-container disruption widens as hauliers join stoppage
items.discovery: India port operations, carrier advisory and empty-equipment flow scan; cross-checked with CMA CGM and Indian trade reporting
items.summary: Empty-container disruption at Mundra has spread from depot operators to road hauliers after APSEZ restricted empty-box nominations to designated yards inside the port SEZ. The Mundra Customs Brokers’ Association estimates about 5,000 containers a day are being held up, while roughly 1,500 transporters have stopped movements.
items.logisticsImpact: Exporters relying on factory stuffing face equipment shortages, missed vessel cut-offs and rollover risk, while importers can face delayed empty returns and detention exposure. CFS stuffing remains available, but the disruption is constraining normal equipment circulation at India’s largest commercial port.

items.title: Hapag-Lloyd sets $1,350 low-water surcharge for Manaus cargo
items.discovery: Amazon River low-water and carrier-cost scan
items.summary: Hapag-Lloyd will apply a $1,350-per-container low-water surcharge to cargo moving to or from Manaus with tariffing dates on or after September 12. The carrier cited falling Amazon River levels and a Western Amazon River Authority outlook indicating a potentially severe dry season in the second half of September.
items.logisticsImpact: Lower river levels reduce navigational flexibility and raise operating costs on the Manaus corridor. Shippers face an immediate landed-cost increase and should plan for possible further capacity, draft or schedule constraints if the dry season intensifies.

items.title: COLI completes multi-voyage move of 14 transformers for Poland’s Baltica 2 wind farm
items.discovery: Heavy-lift, breakbulk and energy project-cargo scan; cross-checked with International Transport Journal
items.summary: COLI Group completed a six-month transport program moving 14 GE Vernova power transformers from Türkiye to Poland for the Baltica 2 offshore wind project. Ten units weighing 110–170 tonnes moved through Gdynia, while four 361-tonne transformers were barged to Władysławowo and handled through a complex RoRo operation.
items.logisticsImpact: The move illustrates the infrastructure and sequencing demands behind renewable-energy project logistics. The heaviest units required chartered vessels, barging, temporary storage and route engineering, including mitigation where bridges could not support the loads.

items.title: Qatari and UAE LNG cargoes transferred ship-to-ship outside Strait of Hormuz
items.discovery: Fresh Gulf energy-shipping and chokepoint workaround scan
items.region: Strait of Hormuz / Middle East / Asia
items.summary: Three LNG cargoes from Qatar and the UAE were transferred ship-to-ship outside the Strait of Hormuz, an unusual workaround aimed at keeping deliveries moving despite severe disruption around the chokepoint. The cargoes included supplies destined for India and Japan.
items.logisticsImpact: Using offshore ship-to-ship transfers for LNG shows how deeply the Hormuz disruption is reshaping normal energy logistics. The workaround adds handling complexity, vessel coordination and marine risk while allowing cargoes to bypass some exposure inside the strait.

items.title: Russian strikes hit export facilities and border crossing in Ukraine's Odesa region
items.discovery: Black Sea export-corridor and port-infrastructure disruption scan
items.summary: Russian overnight attacks damaged export facilities in Ukraine's Odesa region and forced the Orlivka border checkpoint with Romania to suspend processing. The region contains Ukraine's principal Black Sea and Danube export gateways, which are already operating under repeated attack pressure.
items.logisticsImpact: Damage to port and border infrastructure narrows Ukraine's usable export options and can push more cargo toward lower-capacity Danube ports and western rail crossings. Grain and other export flows face higher delay, security and rerouting risk.

items.title: Aqaba transit cargo surges as shippers reroute around Hormuz disruption
items.discovery: Middle East alternate-gateway and overland-routing scan
items.summary: Aqaba Container Terminal reported a 155.1% increase in transit volumes in the first half of 2026 as traders shifted cargo away from Gulf routes exposed to the Strait of Hormuz. A significant share is being trucked roughly 760 km from Aqaba into Iraq instead of moving through Iraq's southern Gulf gateways.
items.logisticsImpact: The shift demonstrates a real modal and gateway substitution rather than a theoretical contingency plan. It creates more demand for Jordan-Iraq trucking and border capacity while giving cargo owners an alternative to Gulf port exposure.

items.title: Hapag-Lloyd applies inland congestion surcharge as low Rhine water cuts barge capacity
items.discovery: European inland-waterway and carrier-surcharge scan
items.summary: Hapag-Lloyd introduced a congestion surcharge for inland container moves routed through Antwerp or Rotterdam as low Rhine water reduces barge capacity and pushes additional demand onto truck and rail. The surcharge took effect September 1 for non-FMC cargo, with FMC-relevant shipments following September 20.
items.logisticsImpact: Low water is now translating directly into carrier charges and constrained inland capacity. Shippers using Rhine-linked gateways should expect higher pre- and on-carriage costs, reduced schedule reliability and pressure on alternative truck and rail options.

items.title: Hong Kong Air Cargo adds weekly Brisbane freighter charter
items.discovery: Asia-Pacific dedicated air-cargo capacity scan
items.summary: Hong Kong Air Cargo launched a weekly round-trip freighter charter between Hong Kong and Brisbane on August 29, adding dedicated cargo capacity between East Asia and Queensland.
items.logisticsImpact: The new service gives shippers another direct freighter option on the Hong Kong-Australia trade and can improve capacity access for time-sensitive and higher-volume cargo that cannot rely solely on passenger belly space.

items.title: Strait of Hormuz commodity vessel transits stay in single digits, data shows
items.discovery: Fresh Hormuz vessel-traffic and chokepoint scan
items.summary: Commodity-vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained in single digits, with preliminary Kpler data showing only five ships transiting on Monday versus a recent 10-day average of about 14. No liquid tankers were among the recorded transits, underscoring how severely normal tanker movement remains constrained.
items.logisticsImpact: Persistently depressed traffic through Hormuz keeps energy and vessel-routing risk elevated. Shippers and carriers remain exposed to higher insurance, fuel and contingency-routing costs, while oil and LNG supply chains face continued uncertainty.

items.title: Canada ends Commercial Driver Registration Program and shifts users toward FAST
items.discovery: North American customs and trusted-trader program scan
items.summary: Effective September 1, CBSA is ending the Commercial Driver Registration Program because of low usage and overlap with the Free and Secure Trade program. Existing CDRP cards remain valid until expiry, while drivers seeking ongoing trusted-trader benefits are being directed to FAST.
items.logisticsImpact: Carriers and cross-border drivers using CDRP need to plan their transition to FAST to preserve access to dedicated lanes and expedited processing for eligible movements. The change matters most on high-volume Canada-US trucking corridors.

items.title: UK outlines 2027 customs transition away from Sevington and Holyhead inland border facilities
items.discovery: UK customs infrastructure and transit-process scan
items.summary: The UK government says customs checks handled through Sevington and Holyhead inland border facilities are expected to transition to port-operator infrastructure from early 2027. Sevington will no longer provide facilities to start and end transit movements once the transition occurs, while Holyhead customs checks are also planned to move into port infrastructure.
items.logisticsImpact: Traders using UK transit procedures will need to adjust operating locations and potentially use border facilities, authorised consignor or consignee services, or transit simplifications. There is no immediate process change, but forwarders should begin mapping affected routings before the 2027 transition.

items.title: US forces strike two Iranian launchers on Iran's Larak island, US official says
items.discovery: Fresh Hormuz maritime-security and chokepoint scan; cross-checked with AP and regional reporting
items.region: Strait of Hormuz / Iran / Middle East
items.summary: U.S. forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island after officials said IRGC personnel were preparing rockets carrying sea mines for the Strait of Hormuz. Iran reported casualties and launched retaliatory attacks. The operation marks a fresh military escalation directly beside the Gulf’s principal commercial shipping lane.
items.logisticsImpact: A renewed mine threat can reverse recent gains in transit confidence almost immediately. Tanker operators, insurers and cargo interests face higher security exposure, possible route delays and renewed uncertainty over Gulf oil, LNG and commercial vessel movements.

items.title: Panama Canal introduces Temporary Booking System Adjustments to Increase Flexibility and Equitable Slot Access
items.discovery: Panama Canal primary operational-advisory scan
items.summary: The Panama Canal is changing Neopanamax booking rules from August 30 for booking dates beginning September 13, offering 63 reservation slots weekly and revised minimum allocations by vessel segment. The Authority says the watershed water deficit persists and warns vessels arriving without reservations may face delays.
items.logisticsImpact: Guaranteed transit increasingly depends on securing a reservation, not simply reaching the canal. Operators face tighter planning requirements, possible auction exposure and schedule risk if unreserved vessels encounter scarce capacity.

items.title: Turkish vessel freed after seizure by pirates, Somali officials say
items.discovery: Gulf of Aden and Somali piracy scan
items.region: Somalia / Gulf of Aden / East Africa
items.summary: Turkish and Somali forces freed the Cameroon-flagged MV LUTUF after it was hijacked off Puntland on August 17, Somali officials said. Four pirate boats were destroyed and 14 suspected pirates were reported killed. The seizure had renewed concern over piracy off Somalia; detailed crew-casualty information was not released.
items.logisticsImpact: A successful rescue does not remove the route risk. Renewed piracy raises security, insurance and routing concerns for vessels using the Gulf of Aden and can add another risk layer to already disrupted Red Sea networks.

items.title: Global container schedule reliability falls to 56.4% in July
items.discovery: Global liner performance and schedule-reliability scan
items.summary: Sea-Intelligence data show global container schedule reliability fell 6.1 percentage points in July to 56.4%, the weakest result of 2026 and the lowest since February 2025. Average delays for late arrivals increased to 6.06 days, the highest since January 2024.
items.logisticsImpact: Planning buffers are widening again across major liner trades. Lower schedule reliability raises inventory, transshipment and delivery-date risk even where nominal vessel capacity remains available.

items.title: Russia extends diesel and marine-fuel export ban through September
items.discovery: Energy trade, bunkering and transport-cost scan
items.summary: Russia extended restrictions on exports of diesel, marine fuel and gas oils by producers through September 30 as refinery disruption and domestic shortages continue. Russia is a major diesel exporter, so another month of restricted supply removes barrels from international markets.
items.logisticsImpact: Reduced Russian middle-distillate exports can tighten regional fuel balances and increase replacement-sourcing and bunkering costs, with possible knock-on effects on trucking, rail and ocean-freight fuel surcharges.

items.title: Asia's diesel exports to Africa jump in August, replace Mideast supply, data shows
items.discovery: Energy trade, tanker-routing and supply-chain sourcing scan
items.summary: Asian diesel exports to Africa rose to a roughly 4.5-year high in August as Middle Eastern supply fell sharply amid regional conflict, Red Sea disruption and lower Saudi refinery output. India and other Asian suppliers have stepped in to replace volumes traditionally sourced from the Gulf.
items.logisticsImpact: The shift is redrawing tanker routes and sourcing patterns for African fuel buyers, increasing voyage distances and exposure to Asian refinery economics while reducing dependence on disrupted Middle Eastern supply.

items.title: Port workers’ strike could hurt Rotterdam port’s reputation among major companies
items.discovery: European port labor and terminal-operations scan
items.summary: Port workers in Rotterdam, Amsterdam and Zeeland plan to stop work from 11:15 a.m. to 7 p.m. on September 4. The Port of Rotterdam expects vessel waiting times to rise, while a port economist warned disruption could take one to two weeks to work through connected logistics networks.
items.logisticsImpact: Even a short stoppage can create vessel bunching, anchorage waits and delayed inland connections. Rotterdam is already dealing with low-water pressure and terminal waits, increasing the chance that recovery extends beyond the strike itself.

items.title: Canada takes next step in potential listing of Roberts Bank Terminal 2 under Building Canada Act
items.discovery: North American port-capacity and infrastructure-permitting scan
items.summary: Canada published formal notice that Roberts Bank Terminal 2 is being considered for national-interest listing under the Building Canada Act, opening public comment through October 1. The proposed three-berth terminal is a core part of plans to expand Vancouver container and export capacity.
items.logisticsImpact: A national-interest listing could streamline federal coordination around one of Canada’s largest prospective container-capacity additions, improving the probability and timing of a major new Pacific gateway and rail-connected trade option.

items.title: General Rate Increase (GRI), US and Canada to the India Subcontinent, Middle East and Africa
items.discovery: Global ocean-freight rate and trade-lane advisory scan
items.region: North America / South Asia / Middle East / Africa
items.summary: A general rate increase took effect August 29 on ocean services from the United States and Canada to the India Subcontinent, Middle East and Africa. C.H. Robinson lists increases of $400 per 20-foot dry container and $800 per 40-foot dry or high-cube container, with an LCL increase as well.
items.logisticsImpact: The filing raises near-term landed-cost pressure across several long-haul trades and gives shippers another reason to recheck contract coverage, validity dates and routing alternatives before booking.

items.title: LCT: Country’s first FDI port project takes off tomorrow
items.discovery: South Asia port-capacity and infrastructure-project scan
items.summary: Construction of Bangladesh’s Laldia Container Terminal is scheduled to begin August 30. The more than $550 million greenfield project at Chattogram is being developed under a DBFOT model and is intended to expand container handling and improve the country’s ability to accommodate larger vessels.
items.logisticsImpact: Laldia is a material capacity project for Bangladesh’s main gateway. Once delivered, larger-vessel access and additional terminal capacity could reduce dependence on constrained existing facilities and improve direct-service economics.

items.title: Klaipėda Port begins largest expansion project in its history
items.discovery: European port-capacity and infrastructure-investment scan
items.summary: Klaipėda Port has begun site preparation for a major southern expansion, with breakwater construction due to start in autumn. The port plans nearly €600 million of investment through 2029, while total project value including private investment is expected to exceed €1 billion.
items.logisticsImpact: The project materially expands Baltic gateway capacity and creates more room for cargo handling, investment and regional trade flows, strengthening Klaipėda's role as an alternative northern European logistics gateway.

items.title: Dredging starts on London Gateway's $473 million fifth berth
items.discovery: European port-capacity and terminal-construction scan
items.summary: DP World’s London Gateway has entered the main dredging phase for its fifth container berth as part of a £350 million expansion. The new deep-water berth is designed for the world’s largest containerships and follows major progress on quay-wall and anchoring works.
items.logisticsImpact: The fifth berth will add deep-water container capacity at a major UK gateway, increasing room to absorb larger vessels and vessel bunching while strengthening routing alternatives in the UK port system.

items.title: CBIC releases Time Release Study 2026 of Jawaharlal Nehru Custom House
items.discovery: South Asia customs, clearance-time and trade-facilitation scan
items.summary: JNCH’s 2026 Time Release Study shows average import release time falling to 65 hours 53 minutes from 72 hours 52 minutes despite a 16% increase in Bills of Entry. AEO cargo averaged 40 hours 40 minutes, compared with 76 hours 59 minutes for non-AEO consignments.
items.logisticsImpact: The figures quantify the operational value of trusted-trader status and earlier clearance preparation. Faster customs processing can reduce dwell and storage, while remaining elapsed time highlights non-customs bottlenecks.

items.title: Ethiopian Cargo begins China-Ethiopia freighter service
items.discovery: Africa-Asia air-cargo capacity scan
items.summary: Ethiopian Cargo has started a freighter service linking Chengdu with Addis Ababa, adding dedicated capacity between western China and its African hub. The route supports Asia-Africa trade and onward connections across Ethiopian Airlines’ cargo network.
items.logisticsImpact: The service adds direct uplift on a China-Africa lane and can improve routing options for time-sensitive, high-value and e-commerce cargo moving through Addis Ababa into regional African markets.

items.title: La Spezia steps up $405m terminal expansion
items.discovery: European port, rail and terminal-equipment scan
items.summary: La Spezia Container Terminal signed €90 million of crane contracts for four ship-to-shore units and 18 yard cranes as part of a €350 million expansion. The future configuration is designed to work three 24,000-TEU vessels simultaneously and increase rail’s share of container movements.
items.logisticsImpact: The investment adds large-vessel handling and rail capacity at a key Italian gateway, potentially improving terminal productivity and inland modal options once the new equipment and Ravano works are completed.
